newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Rostelekom has lower profits.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Rostelekom has lower profits.

text.p: Russian international long-distance provider Rostelekom announced sharply lower first quarter profits on Tuesday, and analysts said the figures presaged an overall decline in 1997 profits though long term prospects remain solid.

AOOT Mezhdugorodnoi i Mezhdunarodnoi Elektricheskoi Svyazi Rostelekom said pre-tax profits to Russian standards on an accruals basis fell to 467.5 billion roubles in the first quarter of the year, from 767.5 billion roubles in 1996.

The telecoms company also posted 1996 pre-tax profits of 1.11 trillion roubles on a cash basis. It said pre-tax profit in 1995 was 1.04 trillion roubles, but did not say on what basis the figure was calculated.

The balance sheet showed first quarter 1997 sales rose to 1.7 trillion roubles from 1.6 trillion roubles in the first quarter of 1996, but analysts said the figure, which was unadjusted for inflation, hid a decline in real revenues.
Analysts said the gloomy financial picture could improve with the release of accounts audited to international standards, but they disagreed on the extent of the difference.

"We're likely to see year-on-year growth in 1996 (to international standards) but looking forward to 1997 we'll see some decline in profits, although not as severe as under Russian standards," said analyst Yuri Krapivin of Renaissance Capital.

But CentreInvest Group analyst Anton Inshutin said 1997 profits to international standards could even grow, although more slowly than in previous years, while Russian figures would show flat or lower profits for the year.

Rostelekom has not released internationally audited 1996 results yet, but expects net profits to rise to about $265 million from $247 million in 1995, and sales to rise to $2.0 billion from $1.78 billion in 1995.

Analysts said declining international rates and flat traffic volumes had cut into first quarter revenues, while agreements on revenue-sharing revised in favour of local domestic telecoms, depreciation charges on assets and rising costs had hit profits.

"(Declining rates) were supposed to be offset by higher traffic, but those expectations have not materialised so far," said Krapivin, citing growth in outgoing international traffic in 1996 of just 0.5 percent compared to 1995.

Inshutin said the results, along with the transfer of the state's controlling stake to Svyazinvest, could affect Rostelekom's plans for a Eurobond this year, for which it has received Standard & Poor's BB- rating.
"It was state ownership that led to the higher than expected rating for Rostelekom," said Inshutin, noting that Russia was given the same rating for its 1996 sovereign Eurobond issue.
"(The first quarter results) could worsen Rostelekom's ability to raise finance at lower rates -- it will have to pay more for the debt."
Krapivin disagreed, however, noting that investors were more likely to focus on rosier international audits.
And analysts doubted Rostelekom equity price would be hit very hard by the results, predicting it would not fall further than by five percent and would in any case rebound rapidly.

"If it doesn't have any influence at all I wouldn't be at all surprised," said Renaissance's Krapivin, citing what he saw as a tendency of Russian shares to appreciate on demand rather than on company fundamentals.
"In the long term Rostelekom is an attractive buy, just because the ultimate economic recovery should result in more robust traffic growth and Rostelekom will benefit from it."
